claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy has a predominantly coarse or untailored microstructure.
The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy has high strength but limited ductility and nonuniform or localized deformation.
The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exhibits rapid localized energy release under dynamic loading.
Moderate cold deformation followed by rapid annealing below the recrystallization temperature will induce a high density of nanoscale twins in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The treatment will produce a fine, spatially uniform dispersion of deformation twins within the grains.
Twin boundaries impede dislocation motion and can thereby contribute to strengthening.
The nanoscale twins refine the effective microstructure.
The induced twins enable combined dislocation-slip and twinning deformation pathways.
Twinning impedes localized dislocation slip and delays shear localization.
The combined twinning and slip response promotes distributed plasticity and more uniform deformation.
Multiple twinning systems can enhance ductility while preserving high strength.
The treated refractory high-entropy alloy will have greater ductility than the untreated alloy under quasi-static and dynamic loading.
The treated alloy will deform more homogeneously than the untreated alloy under dynamic loading.
The treatment will maintain high yield and ultimate strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will preserve impact-induced energy release relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed benefits should persist from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures and under both quasi-static and high-strain-rate loading.
The improvement requires an alloy chemistry and phase state that permit twin formation.
Alloys that do not inherently favor twinning may not exhibit the proposed benefit.
A same-composition treated-versus-untreated comparison using tensile and high-strain-rate tests, TEM, and EBSD is proposed to test the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant ductility and deformation-uniformity improvement while maintaining comparable strength and energy release would refute the hypothesis.
